case_studies.title: KRCA: An Efficient Root Cause Analysis System in Hyper-Scale Microservice Systems via Agentic AI
case_studies.abstract: Hyper-scale microservice systems have become the standard infrastructure for large-scale Internet companies. These systems consist of numerous loosely coupled microservices that evolve independently through continuous development and deployment. Such complexity makes failures unavoidable, necessitating efficient Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to help Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) quickly localize root cause services and classify failure types. However, existing RCA methods often struggle to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale of these systems. In this paper, we present KRCA, an end-
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of efficient root cause analysis in complex microservice systems by building a system called KRCA that uses AI to help identify and classify failures. The result is a more efficient way for Site Reliability Engineers to localize root cause services and classify failure types. This improves the reliability of large-scale internet systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage hyper-scale microservice systems, here is what to do: assess your current root cause analysis process, consider implementing an AI-powered solution like KRCA, and evaluate its potential to reduce downtime and improve system reliability.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: KRCA presents an agentic AI system for root cause analysis in hyper-scale microservice systems, which is not commonly seen in IT infrastructure. However, it doesn't reveal a completely unexpected approach. IT Relevance: This paper directly affects how IT engineers, especially SREs, work in deploying and maintaining complex microservice systems. Value 90 days: KRCA could be used to automate root cause analysis, and potentially improve the reliability of IT systems within 90 days. Relevance Tag: DevOps automation and SRE tooling.

case_studies.title: Risk Architecture for AI-Native Engineering Teams: An Organizational Framework for Agentic System Governance
case_studies.abstract: Engineering management research has produced mature frameworks for software risk: ownership by feature, escalation by severity, and assurance by test coverage. These frameworks implicitly assume deterministic behavior, discrete and auditable change events, and clear component-to-owner mappings. Teams that build and operate agentic AI systems violate all three assumptions at once: outputs are probabilistic, systems take autonomous multi-step actions, and the risk surface mutates silently between deployments. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of managing risk in AI systems by creating a framework for agentic system governance, which addresses the unique challenges of probabilistic outputs and autonomous actions in AI systems, resulting in a new approach to risk management. The authors built an organizational framework that adapts traditional software risk management to the needs of AI-native engineering teams. This framework helps teams manage the mutating risk surface of AI systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI or machine learning infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current risk management processes to ensure they account for probabilistic outputs and autonomous actions, assess your team's ability to adapt to mutating risk surfaces, and consider adopting a framework that addresses these unique challenges. This flags a risk: if your org uses AI systems, check your governance and risk management processes immediately to ensure they are adequate. Not directly applicable to non-AI cloud infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: EgoSafetyBench: A Diagnostic Egocentric Video Benchmark for Evaluating Embodied VLMs as Runtime Safety Guards
case_studies.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are now proposed as runtime safety guards for embodied agents in homes and factories. A deployable guard must catch genuinely unsafe situations while avoiding unnecessary intervention on routine but superficially alarming activity, a distinction that binary safety benchmarks obscure. We introduce EgoSafetyBench, an egocentric video benchmark of 1,200 robot-view scenarios annotated at half-second granularity, to evaluate VLMs as streaming guards across two tracks. The situational track (800 scenarios) spans four families, from routine and safe-but-suspicious scenes
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating the effectiveness of vision-language models as safety guards in homes and factories by creating a diagnostic benchmark called EgoSafetyBench. The result is a benchmark that can evaluate these models' ability to distinguish between genuinely unsafe situations and routine but superficially alarming activity. This is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work. No immediate action is required for IT managers.

case_studies.title: AgentsCAD: Automated Design for Manufacturing of FDM Parts via Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning and Geometric Feature Recognition
case_studies.abstract: Parts manufactured with Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) often require Design for Additive Manufacturing (DFAM) modifications to ensure printability, structural integrity, and reduced post-processing. Current slicers identify defects such as steep overhangs but are unable to modify the underlying geometry. This work presents AgentsCAD, a multi-agent system that bridges raw boundary-representation (B-Rep) geometry and Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning to automate targeted DFM. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of ensuring printability and structural integrity of FDM parts by automating Design for Additive Manufacturing modifications. The team built AgentsCAD, a multi-agent system that uses LLM reasoning and geometric feature recognition. The result is an automated workflow that can modify the underlying geometry of FDM parts for better manufacturing outcomes.

case_studies.title: The Future of NLP may not be at NLP Conferences: Scholarly Migration Patterns in Natural Language Processing
case_studies.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has traditionally been published in its core disciplinary venues like ACL. However, advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to a blurring of the disciplinary lines between NLP and general Machine Learning (ML), with authors regularly publishing in venues from both fields. Here, we ask whether the disciplinary center of gravity is shifting. It found that established authors are shifting where they publish their work. This study is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: Next-Generation Agentic Reinforcement Learning Systems Enable Self-Evolving Agents
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents are rapidly being deployed in production, including coding assistants, customer-support chatbots, and scientific research assistants, yet they remain fundamentally static in enterprise deployment. The LLM weights, system prompts, tool repertoires, and in-context harnesses are frozen at deployment time, and any improvement requires a manual loop of human-curated data collection, offline fine-tuning, modification of the agentic paradigm, and re-deployment. Recent work on self-evolving agents, such as OpenClaw for individual users, indicates that the next leap in agent capability will
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of static Large Language Model (LLM) agents by creating self-evolving agents that can improve without manual intervention. The researchers built a next-generation agentic reinforcement learning system that enables LLM agents to evolve over time. The result is a more dynamic and capable agent that can adapt to new situations.

case_studies.title: Bayesian Uncertainty Propagation for Agentic RAG Pipelines: A Proof-of-Concept Study on Multi-Hop Question Answering
case_studies.abstract: Trustworthy deployment of Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems requires mechanisms for estimating when multi-stage reasoning pipelines may fail. This paper presents an uncertainty-aware Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework in which planner, evaluator and generator stages produce uncertainty signals derived from semantic divergence and generator self-evaluation. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of estimating when multi-stage reasoning pipelines may fail in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems. The researchers built an uncertainty-aware framework that produces and propagates uncertainty signals through a Bayesian Network. The result is a system that can estimate system-level uncertainty and identify potential failure points.
